questions.q: How much of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions comes from raising livestock?
a: About 20 percent
About 5 percent
About 35 percent
About 50 percent
questions.why: The overview and Lesson 3 put livestock at roughly 20 percent, compared with 13 percent for all transportation.

questions.q: Why does animal farming require so much land?
a: Farmers also need vast areas to grow feed for the animals
Animals must be kept far away from cities
Each animal needs its own enclosed pasture
Land is left empty to recover between herds
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains that land is needed for the livestock and for the crops that feed them, which drives rainforest clearing.

questions.q: What does the summary say would happen if grain fed to livestock went to people instead?
a: World hunger could be overcome quickly
Meat would become cheaper in rich countries
Farmers would need more water than before
Crop yields would fall in the short term
questions.why: Oppenlander argues that redirecting livestock grain to humans could feed everyone and end world hunger in no time.

questions.q: Why is methane from livestock especially troubling?
a: It traps roughly 30 times more heat than carbon dioxide
It stays in the atmosphere for many centuries
It blocks sunlight from reaching crops
It dissolves easily into drinking water
questions.why: Lesson 3 notes that methane is about 30 times more potent as a heat-trapping gas than carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What makes livestock waste especially dangerous?
a: It carries hormones, antibiotics and pesticides into water
It is too dry to break down naturally
It is stored safely in sealed tanks
It only affects the soil near the farm
questions.why: The summary says the waste is full of drugs and chemicals that reach water systems and re-enter the food chain.
